title: Open-Source LLM History: GPT-2 to Kimi K3 (2026)
summary: Open-source LLM history, 2019 to 2026: GPT-2's 1.5B release, LLaMA, Mistral, DeepSeek R1, Qwen, gpt-oss and the 2.8T Kimi K3, with dates, sizes and licenses.
body_markdown:
Open-source large language models went from "too dangerous to release" to **larger and more capable than most people thought possible in the open** — in about six years. In 2019, OpenAI held back the full weights of GPT-2, a 1.5-billion-parameter model, worried it was too risky to publish. In July 2026, a Chinese lab shipped **Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model** at frontier level, with the full weights posted on Hugging Face on July 27 for anyone to download. Three months later, even Meta, which had gone closed in April 2026, came back with the 816-billion-parameter Muse Spark Open.


How did we get from one to the other? Which models actually mattered, who built them, and what's the real difference between "open source" and "open weight" — a distinction almost every article gets wrong? This is the complete timeline. 🧬


> **TL;DR:** Open-source LLMs evolved from **GPT-2's cautious 2019 release** → the truly-open era of **EleutherAI and BLOOM (2021–22)** → **Meta's LLaMA (2023)** detonating the ecosystem → **Mistral** bringing mixture-of-experts to open weights → **DeepSeek's 2025 cost shock** → a Chinese open-weight surge ( **Qwen, Kimi, GLM** ) that shrank the gap to the closed frontier to a matter of months. Most "open" models are technically **open weight** , not fully open source.[See the 10 best open-source LLMs ranked →](https://www.taskade.com/blog/open-source-llms)


## What Is the History of Open-Source LLMs?


The history of open-source LLMs runs from OpenAI's staged release of **GPT-2 in 2019** (1.5 billion parameters) through EleutherAI and BLOOM (2021 to 2022), Meta's LLaMA (2023), Mistral's open mixture-of-experts models, DeepSeek-R1 (January 2025) and OpenAI's gpt-oss (August 2025), to the 2026 trillion-parameter era of **Kimi K3** , Qwen3.8 and Muse Spark Open.


In numbers: the largest open model grew from 1.5 billion parameters in November 2019 to 2.8 trillion in July 2026, an increase of more than 1,800 times in under seven years. The licenses moved the other way, from "too risky to publish" to MIT and Apache 2.0, and then in 2026 to MIT-style licenses with one extra clause for very large API businesses. This guide covers each era in order, with the exact dates, parameter counts and licenses taken from each lab's own announcement, model card or paper.

## What "Open-Source LLM" Actually Means (and Why "Open Weight" Is More Accurate)


Most models people call "open source" are actually **open weight** — a crucial difference. An **open-weight** model releases its trained parameters so you can download, run, and fine-tune it. A truly **open-source** model, by the[Open Source Initiative's](https://opensource.org/ai) 2024 definition, releases the weights *plus* the training code, information about the data, and a license with no usage restrictions.


The Linux Foundation's **Model Openness Framework** — created by its Global CTO of AI, Matt White — grades this on three levels, and it's the cleanest way to think about the spectrum:


Level What's released Term people use Examples


**Open Science (Class I)** Weights + code + raw training data + checkpoints + paper Fully open source BLOOM, OLMo, LLM360


**Open Tooling (Class II)** Weights + full training/eval code, no raw data Open source (loosely) Some research releases


**Open Model (Class III)** Just the weights + light docs **Open weight** Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM


Almost every "open" model you've heard of — Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi — sits in that bottom row: **open weight** . That's still enormously valuable (you can run and adapt them), but it's not the same as fully reproducible. Matt White's own worry, after touring China's labs in 2026, was about disclosure shrinking:


> "The research papers have shrunk and then become technical reports. And so there's not enough disclosure in a lot of these technical reports to be able to go and replicate the research."
>
>
> — Matt White, Linux Foundation


### What Is the OSI Open Source AI Definition (OSAID)?


The **Open Source AI Definition 1.0** is the Open Source Initiative's rule for when an AI system counts as open source. The OSI published it on October 28, 2024, after two years of drafts. It applies the four classic software freedoms to AI: anyone must be able to **use** the system for any purpose, **study** how it works, **modify** it, and **share** it, with or without changes.


To make those freedoms real, the definition asks for the "preferred form to make modifications." For a machine-learning model that means three parts, all under OSI-approved terms:


- **Parameters:** the weights, and ideally checkpoints from key training stages.
- **Code:** the complete code used to process data, train, and run the model.
- **Data information:** a description of the training data detailed enough that a skilled person could build a substantially equivalent system, with a list of public and third-party sources.


The data rule is the one most labs fail. The definition does not demand that every training document be published, because some data cannot be shared legally. It does demand enough detail to rebuild something equivalent. The[full text on opensource.org](https://opensource.org/ai/open-source-ai-definition) is short and worth reading.


### Which Famous Models Pass the OSI Definition?


The OSI does not certify models one by one. During its validation phase it did test a set of real models against the draft, and the results show how rare full openness is:

Source: the[OSI's OSAID FAQ](https://opensource.org/ai/faq) . In February 2025 the OSI also wrote that the Llama licenses are not open source because they restrict who can use the model and for what. That is why this guide says "open weight" for most of the famous models and saves "open source" for the few that publish everything. ### What Does "Open Weights" Look Like on Disk?


Andrej Karpathy's well-known talk describes an open-weight model in the simplest terms: a parameters file and a small program that runs it. In his example, Llama 2 70B is a file of about 140 GB, since each of its 70 billion parameters takes 2 bytes, plus a few hundred lines of code. Everything that makes the model useful lives in that one file, which is why releasing it, or not, is such a big decision. The first part of the talk explains it in a few minutes.

## Before GPT-2: When Open Research Was the Default (2013 to 2018)


Before 2019, nobody asked whether a language model was "safe to release." Research labs published papers, code and weights as a matter of course, and the field moved fast because of it.


- **2013:** Google released **word2vec** as open-source code with pretrained word vectors. It was the first time many developers used a model that "knew" what words meant.
- **June 2017:** eight Google researchers published *Attention Is All You Need* , the paper that introduced the **transformer** , the architecture every model in this history uses. Read our wiki entry on the[transformer](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/transformer) and the[attention mechanism](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/attention-mechanism) for the basics.
- **June 2018:** OpenAI published **GPT-1** , a 117-million-parameter transformer, together with its code and weights.
- **November 2018:** Google open-sourced **BERT** with weights under Apache 2.0. BERT reads text instead of writing it, so it is not a chatbot ancestor, but it proved that one pretrained model could be fine-tuned for hundreds of tasks.


So "open" was the starting point. The surprise of 2019 was a lab deciding to close a door that had always been open. For the wider arc, read our[history of computing](https://www.taskade.com/blog/history-of-computing) and the story of[GPT from GPT-1 to GPT-6](https://www.taskade.com/blog/what-is-gpt) .


## 2019: GPT-2 and the Cautious Birth of Open Models


The modern open-model story starts with a decision *not* to release. On February 14, 2019, OpenAI announced **GPT-2** , a 1.5-billion-parameter model described in the paper *Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners* , but held back the full weights, worrying openly that the model could be used to mass-produce fake text. It released the full 1.5B weights only on **November 5, 2019** , after a staged rollout and a partner study, published in August 2019 as *Release Strategies and the Social Impacts of Language Models* , found no strong evidence of misuse.


The myth-correction matters: **GPT-2 was not "fully open" at launch.** It was a careful, staged release — the first time a major lab treated a language model as something whose openness was a *policy question* , not a default. That framing has shaped every open-vs-closed debate since. (If you want the mechanics of how these models work at all, our explainer on[how large language models work](https://www.taskade.com/blog/how-do-llms-work) is the primer.)


### When Was GPT-2 Released? The Four-Stage Rollout


GPT-2 was released in four stages over nine months in 2019, from the 124-million-parameter model on February 14 to the full 1.5-billion-parameter model on November 5. OpenAI published each size with a blog post, and it shared the larger sizes with research partners before the public got them.

The "first reported as" column explains a common source of confusion. The original paper listed 117M, 345M, 762M and 1,542M. OpenAI later corrected the counts to 124M, 355M, 774M and 1,558M, which is why you will see both sets of numbers quoted for the same models.


### How Many Parameters Does GPT-2 Have?


GPT-2 has **1.5 billion parameters** in its full size, 1,558 million to be exact. It is a decoder-only transformer with 48 layers and a 1,024-token context window. OpenAI trained it on **WebText** , about 40 GB of text from roughly 8 million web pages that Reddit users had linked to.

### Why Did OpenAI Hold GPT-2 Back?


OpenAI held GPT-2 back because it worried the model could produce convincing fake news, spam and abuse at a scale no one had seen. The February 2019 post said the lab would not release "the dataset, training code, or GPT-2 model weights" for the largest model, and called the plan "an experiment in responsible disclosure."


The partner research that followed gave the decision some data. Researchers at Cornell asked people to rate the credibility of GPT-2 text: the 1.5B model scored 6.91 out of 10, the 774M model 6.72, and the 355M model 6.07. OpenAI also built a detector that caught about 95% of 1.5B outputs. In the end, the lab said it had seen "no strong evidence of misuse" and published everything.


Two things are worth noticing. First, the debate GPT-2 started, about whether a model is too dangerous to share, is the same debate every lab still has about frontier weights. Second, the license OpenAI chose was a **Modified MIT License** that asked users to say when content came from GPT-2. Six years later, Moonshot AI shipped Kimi K2 under a modified MIT license with an attribution clause of its own. The idea came full circle.


### GPT-2's Afterlife: From $43,000 to $672


GPT-2 is still the standard teaching model for open LLMs. Andrej Karpathy has estimated that OpenAI's original run used 32 TPU v3 chips for about a week, roughly $43,000 of compute. In July 2024 his open-source llm.c project reproduced the full 1.5B GPT-2 on one 8x H100 node in 24 hours for about **$672** , thanks to better GPUs, better software and cleaner data. In August 2019, two Brown University graduate students had already shown the "too dangerous" model could be rebuilt from public information, when they released their own 1.5B replication, OpenGPT-2.


That cost curve is the hidden engine of this whole history: every year, the model that once needed a frontier lab gets cheaper for everyone. Karpathy's four-hour walkthrough rebuilds the 124M GPT-2 from an empty file.


## 2021–2022: The Truly-Open Era — EleutherAI, OPT, and BLOOM


The first genuinely open GPT-3-class models didn't come from a big lab — they came from a volunteer collective. **EleutherAI** released **GPT-Neo** (March 2021) and **GPT-J-6B** , then **GPT-NeoX-20B** (2022), reverse-engineering GPT-3-style capability and publishing everything. For the first time, anyone could download a large, capable model and its code.


Two 2022 releases pushed openness to its high-water mark:


- **Meta OPT-175B** — Meta's attempt to open-source a GPT-3-scale model, released with training logs and a research license.
- **BLOOM** — the crown jewel of the truly-open era. Built by **BigScience** , a collaboration of **over 1,000 researchers** , BLOOM was a **176-billion-parameter** model trained on **46 natural languages and 13 programming languages** , released with open weights, code, and full documentation. By the Model Openness Framework, BLOOM is one of the few models that reaches "Open Science" — the genuinely fully-open tier.


### EleutherAI and The Pile: A Discord Server Rebuilds GPT-3


EleutherAI started in July 2020 as a Discord server, founded by Connor Leahy, Sid Black and Leo Gao, with one goal: build an open replication of GPT-3, which OpenAI had announced that summer as an API only. Its first big contribution was not a model but a dataset. **The Pile** , released on December 31, 2020, packed 825 GiB of text from 22 sources, including books, papers, code and web text, and it became the standard open training set for the next three years.


EleutherAI logo by Sid Black. Image: Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 4.0.


The models came next, each one larger:


- **GPT-Neo** (March 2021): 1.3B and 2.7B parameters, trained on The Pile, MIT license.
- **GPT-J-6B** (June 2021): built by Ben Wang and Aran Komatsuzaki on Google TPUs with the Mesh Transformer JAX library, Apache 2.0. For about a year it was the most capable model anyone could download.
- **GPT-NeoX-20B** (February 2022): 20 billion parameters, Apache 2.0, trained on GPUs donated by the cloud company CoreWeave.
- **Pythia** (2023): a suite of 16 models from 70 million to 12 billion parameters, each released with intermediate checkpoints, built so scientists could study how a model learns over training. Pythia is one of the models that passed the OSI definition.


### OPT-175B: Big Tech Opens a GPT-3-Sized Model


Meta released **OPT** (Open Pretrained Transformer) on May 3, 2022. Sizes from 125 million to 66 billion parameters were free to download, and the full 175B model was available to researchers on request under a noncommercial license. Meta also published a logbook of the training run, with every crash and restart, which was rare honesty for a large lab. OPT matched GPT-3 on many benchmarks, but its license kept it inside research.


### BLOOM: 1,000 Researchers and a French Supercomputer


**BLOOM** , released on July 12, 2022, is the high-water mark of the truly open era. The BigScience workshop, coordinated by Hugging Face, brought together more than 1,000 researchers from dozens of countries. They trained the 176-billion-parameter model for about four months on 384 Nvidia A100 GPUs in the **Jean Zay** supercomputer near Paris, with compute time granted by the French government.


BLOOM covered 46 natural languages and 13 programming languages, including languages such as Swahili, Yoruba and Vietnamese that most large models of the time left out. It shipped under the **BigScience RAIL License 1.0** , an early "responsible AI" license that allowed commercial use but banned a list of harmful uses. That use-based list is why the OSI later said BLOOM would pass its definition only with license changes.


### GLM-130B and Galactica: Two Endings for 2022


Two more releases closed the year. In August 2022, Tsinghua University released **GLM-130B** , a 130-billion-parameter bilingual Chinese and English model. Its team later founded Zhipu AI, now Z.ai, which makes the GLM models that sit near the top of the open rankings in 2026. In November 2022, Meta released **Galactica** , a 120B model for science, with a public demo. Users quickly showed it inventing confident, fake citations, and Meta took the demo down after three days. The lesson about[AI hallucinations](https://www.taskade.com/blog/what-are-ai-hallucinations) stuck.

This era proved the community *could* build at scale. What it hadn't yet proved was that open models could be genuinely *useful* . That changed in 2023.


## 2023: Llama Changes Everything (and the "Open" Debate Begins)


**Meta's LLaMA** is the single most important release in this history, because it turned open weights into an *ecosystem* . **LLaMA 1** (February 24, 2023) came in 7B to 65B sizes and — after the weights leaked online — detonated a wave of community fine-tunes (Alpaca, Vicuna, and hundreds more). **Llama 2** (July 2023) made it official, shipping with a license that permitted commercial use.


### Why ChatGPT Made Open Models Urgent


ChatGPT launched on November 30, 2022, and changed the question. Before it, open models were research tools. After it, every company wanted a chat model of its own, and most did not want to send their data to one vendor's API. That demand is what turned the next open release into an event. For the closed side of the same story, read the[history of OpenAI and ChatGPT](https://www.taskade.com/blog/openai-chatgpt-history) .


### Did LLaMA Leak? The 4chan Torrent of March 2023


Yes. Meta announced **LLaMA** (Large Language Model Meta AI) on February 24, 2023, in four sizes: 7B, 13B, 33B and 65B parameters. The two larger models trained on 1.4 trillion tokens of public data, and Meta's paper reported that the 13B model beat the 175B GPT-3 on most benchmarks. Access was by application only, under a noncommercial research license.


On March 3, 2023, about a week later, someone posted a torrent of the weights on 4chan. Within days the files were everywhere, and Meta's takedown requests could not pull them back. The leak did what no press release could. It put a strong base model in the hands of every hobbyist, student and startup at the same moment.


The animal that gave the model its name. Photo: Alex Proimos / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0.

What followed was the fastest burst of open AI work up to that point. Most of it took days, not months, and cost less than a used laptop.

In May 2023 a Google engineer's internal memo leaked under the title *"We Have No Moat, And Neither Does OpenAI."* Its argument was that open-source fine-tunes were closing the gap faster than any big lab could. The memo overstated the case, but it captured the mood. For the first time, the open community was setting the pace.


### Falcon, MPT and the First Truly Commercial Open Models


LLaMA's license did not allow commercial use, so the first open models a business could ship came from elsewhere. MosaicML's **MPT-7B** arrived in May 2023 under Apache 2.0. The Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi released **Falcon-40B** the same month. It went to the top of the Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard, and on May 31, 2023 TII moved it to Apache 2.0. Its larger sibling, **Falcon 180B** , followed in September 2023 under a custom TII license.


Hugging Face became the meeting place for all of it. Its model hub, its leaderboard and its open-source Transformers library turned "download a model" into one line of code. Our guide to[fine-tuning versus RAG](https://www.taskade.com/blog/fine-tuning-vs-rag) covers what all those community fine-tunes were trying to do.


Hugging Face became the default home for open weights. Photo: Jernej Furman / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0.


### Llama 2: Open Weights Go Commercial (July 18, 2023)


**Llama 2** arrived on July 18, 2023, with Microsoft as a launch partner. It came in 7B, 13B and 70B sizes, trained on 2 trillion tokens with a 4,096-token context window, plus chat versions tuned with human feedback. The big change was the license. The **Llama 2 Community License** allowed commercial use, with one headline exception: a company whose products had more than **700 million monthly active users** in the month before release had to ask Meta for a separate license. In practice, that clause excluded only a handful of rivals.


Code Llama followed on August 24, 2023. By the end of the year, "built on Llama" was the most common line in an open-model card.


But Llama also started the argument that still runs today.


### Is Llama Really Open Source?


**No, not by the strict definition.** The Open Source Initiative classifies Llama as **source-available** or **open weight** , not open source, for two reasons: the **Llama Community License** restricts use above **700 million monthly active users** , and it ships with an acceptable-use policy plus undisclosed training data. Critics call this "openwashing" — marketing a restricted release as open. Defenders point out that for 99.9% of developers, Llama was *effectively* open and did more to democratize LLMs than any purely-open model. Both are true, which is why the debate never fully resolves.


## 2023–2024: Mistral and the Mixture-of-Experts Moment


A French startup made the next leap. **Mistral AI** , founded by ex-Meta and DeepMind researchers Arthur Mensch, Guillaume Lample, and Timothée Lacroix, released **Mistral 7B** (September 2023) under the fully-permissive **Apache 2.0** license — no MAU clause, no strings. Then came **Mixtral 8x7B** (December 2023), which brought **mixture-of-experts (MoE)** to open weights: instead of running the whole model for every token, MoE activates only a few specialist "experts," delivering big-model quality at small-model cost.


MoE is the architecture that made everything after it possible. Every trillion-parameter open model since — DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM — is an MoE. Mistral proved you could ship it in the open, and that Europe had a frontier lab of its own.


### The Magnet Link Release


Mistral AI was founded in Paris in April 2023. Arthur Mensch came from Google DeepMind, and Guillaume Lample and Timothée Lacroix came from Meta, where they had worked on LLaMA. Five months later, on September 27, 2023, the company released Mistral 7B in an unusual way: a post on X with nothing but a BitTorrent magnet link. No blog, no demo, no waitlist.


The 7.3-billion-parameter model beat Llama 2 13B on Mistral's reported benchmarks, and it shipped under Apache 2.0, with no user threshold and no use policy. On December 8, 2023, Mistral posted another bare magnet link. This one was **Mixtral 8x7B** : eight expert networks per layer, two chosen for each token, 46.7 billion parameters in total and about 12.9 billion used per token. Mistral reported that it matched or beat Llama 2 70B and GPT-3.5 on most benchmarks while running at the speed of a much smaller model.


Arthur Mensch, co-founder and CEO of Mistral AI. Photo: Slush / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 4.0.


### Mistral's License Path After Mixtral


Mistral's later releases show how unsettled open licensing still was. Mixtral 8x22B (April 2024, 141B total, 39B active) stayed on Apache 2.0. Mistral Large 2 (July 2024) moved to a research-only license for its weights. ## How Mixture of Experts Took Over Open Models


A **mixture-of-experts (MoE)** model splits each layer's feed-forward network into many smaller "experts" and adds a small router that sends each token to only a few of them. The model can store a huge amount of knowledge in its total parameters while each token pays the compute cost of only the active ones. That trade is why almost every open flagship released since 2025 is an MoE. The last famous dense giant was Llama 3.1 405B in July 2024. Read our wiki entry on[mixture of experts](https://www.taskade.com/wiki/ai/mixture-of-experts) for the full mechanics.


The open MoE lineage got sparser every year. Mixtral used a quarter of its parameters per token. Kimi K3 uses less than 4%. That shrinking fraction is the single biggest reason a 2.8-trillion-parameter model can be served at a price close to a mid-size closed model.

## Why Are Chinese Open-Source Models Winning? The Debate


This is the most-discussed — and most-contested — question in the field, so let's be precise about what's argued versus what's settled.


**The popular thesis:** US GPU export controls (restricting the best chips to Chinese buyers) pushed Chinese labs toward **software-efficiency breakthroughs** — mixture-of-experts, latent attention, and cheaper training recipes — because "when you can't throw more compute at a problem, you find smarter solutions" (Matt White's framing). Layer on a culture of publishing and a **"borrow-and-build" chain** — one lab's technique (like DeepSeek's GRPO reinforcement-learning method) gets adopted and improved by the next — and you get rapid, compounding open progress.


**The dissent is serious and named.** Analysts including Gregory Allen (CSIS) argue that *motivation* to localize is not the same as *acceleration* , and that some Chinese chip-independence efforts predate the controls. Chris McGuire (CFR) argues the US chip lead is actually *widening* . And Anthropic's Dario Amodei argues DeepSeek's efficiency was "an expected point on an ongoing cost-reduction curve," not a resource-constraint miracle.


A careful reading of the download data supports humility on both sides. By one 2026 analysis, Chinese models edged ahead of US models in the share of downloads *of newly released models* — but that measures a rolling 12-month window, and on an all-time basis US models still dominate downloads. The honest summary: **Chinese labs drove much of the open-weight momentum in 2025–26, the technical contributions are real, and the geopolitical cause is genuinely debated.** (And a note on attribution: the widely used **Muon** optimizer originated in the international open-source community, not with any single lab or country — cite ideas by their lineage, not a flag.)

## Open vs Closed: How Big Is the Gap in 2026?


The gap has never been smaller. On public benchmarks, the best open-weight models trail the top proprietary systems by a **small and shrinking margin** — often described in 2026 as a matter of a few months rather than the year-plus gap of 2023. Independent reviewers who tested Kimi K3 at launch placed it at or near frontier level for agentic coding, and one summed up the moment bluntly: *"Open-source AI is no longer a few months behind the closed frontier models."*


Two honest caveats keep this from becoming hype. First, **the very hardest reasoning tasks** still tend to favor the top proprietary models. Second, **capability is not reliability** — open frontier models can be slower, more token-hungry, and flakier on long runs than their polished closed rivals. The gap in raw capability is nearly closed; the gap in *dependability* is still real, and it's the reason[AI-generated apps break](https://www.taskade.com/blog/why-ai-generated-apps-break) more often than their demos suggest.

## Open-Source LLM License History: Five Eras in Seven Years


Open-model licenses went through five eras: withheld weights (2019), research-only licenses (2022 to early 2023), community licenses with a user threshold (Llama 2, 2023), plain Apache 2.0 and MIT (Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek-R1, 2023 to 2025), and in 2026, MIT-style licenses with a clause for large model-as-a-service businesses.


The 2026 "MaaS clause" is new enough that most license guides miss it. The licenses read like MIT for nearly everyone: you can download, modify, fine-tune, sell products and build apps. The extra terms bite only when a company resells raw model access through an API and earns above a revenue line. We read each license file on Hugging Face:

## The Hardware Story: From Laptops to Trillion-Parameter Racks


Open weights only matter if someone can run them, so the hardware story runs in parallel with the model story. Between 2023 and 2026 two things happened at once: software tricks shrank mid-size models enough to run on a laptop, and the largest open models grew so big that only a full rack of data-center GPUs can hold them.


### How Did Open Models Get Small Enough for a Laptop?


**Quantization** stores each parameter in fewer bits. A model trained at 16-bit precision uses 2 bytes per parameter; at 4-bit it uses half a byte, a quarter of the memory, with a small loss in quality. Three open projects made this normal:


Date Milestone What it changed


June 2021 LoRA (Microsoft research) Fine-tune a model by training small add-on matrices instead of every weight


March 10, 2023 llama.cpp (Georgi Gerganov) Run LLaMA on a MacBook CPU with 4-bit weights, in plain C and C++


May 2023 QLoRA (University of Washington) Fine-tune a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU


June 2023 vLLM and PagedAttention (UC Berkeley) Serve many users per GPU by managing the context cache like virtual memory


August 2023 GGUF format One file holds weights and settings, the standard for local models


December 2023 Apple MLX Run and fine-tune models on Apple silicon


August 2025 gpt-oss in MXFP4 A frontier lab ships native 4-bit weights; the 120B model fits one 80 GB GPU


July 2026 Kimi K3 in MXFP4 A 2.8T model trained with 4-bit in mind (quantization-aware training), about 1.56 TB on disk

### Why Total Parameters, Not Active Ones, Set the Hardware Bill


A mixture-of-experts model runs only a few experts per token, so people often assume it needs only a little memory. It does not. When a server handles many users at once, almost every expert is in use at some instant, and swapping experts in and out of memory would wreck response times. So the GPUs must hold **all** the weights. That is why Kimi K3, with about 104 billion active parameters, still needs a node of eight Nvidia B300 GPUs with 288 GB of memory each, and does not fit on eight H100s with 80 GB each.


An Nvidia H100. DeepSeek trained V3 on the H800, a version Nvidia made for the Chinese market under US export rules. Photo: Geekerwan / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 3.0.


Hosts split such a model across GPUs in two main ways. **Tensor parallelism** cuts every layer into slices across eight GPUs, which gives the best latency for one user. **Expert parallelism** keeps attention split but places whole experts on specific GPUs, which serves more users per node. ## 💬 Frequently Asked Questions About Open-Source LLMs


What was the first open-source LLM?


There's no clean answer. GPT-2 (2019) is often cited, but its full weights were withheld until November 2019, so it wasn't fully open at launch. EleutherAI's GPT-Neo and GPT-J (2021) were the first genuinely open GPT-3-class models, and BLOOM (2022) was the most fully open early release.


When was GPT-2 released?


OpenAI announced GPT-2 on February 14, 2019, with a 124M model. It released the 355M model in May 2019, the 774M model on August 20, 2019, and the full 1.5-billion-parameter model with code and weights on November 5, 2019.


What size was the full GPT-2 model?


The full GPT-2 has 1.5 billion parameters (1,558M), 48 layers and a 1,024-token context window, trained on about 40 GB of web text from roughly 8 million pages. The smaller versions have 124M, 355M and 774M parameters, first reported as 117M, 345M and 762M.


Why did OpenAI not release GPT-2 at first?


OpenAI worried GPT-2 could mass-produce fake or abusive text, so it ran a staged release and studied misuse with partners. It found no strong evidence of misuse and published the full model nine months later.


Did OpenAI release an open-weight model after GPT-2?


Yes. gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b arrived on August 5, 2025 under Apache 2.0, OpenAI's first open-weight language models since GPT-2. The 120b model has about 117 billion total and 5.1 billion active parameters.


Did the original LLaMA weights leak?


Yes. Meta released LLaMA to approved researchers on February 24, 2023, and a torrent of the weights appeared on 4chan on March 3, 2023. The leak set off Alpaca, Vicuna, llama.cpp and thousands of community fine-tunes.


What's the difference between open source and open weight?


Open weight means you get the downloadable parameters. Open source (by the OSI's 2024 definition) means weights plus training code, data information, and an unrestricted license. Most popular "open" models — Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi — are technically open weight.


Is Llama open source?


Not strictly. The OSI classifies it as source-available/open weight because of the 700-million-MAU clause, an acceptable-use policy, and undisclosed training data — though it's freely usable for almost everyone.


Can I download and use DeepSeek models commercially?


Largely yes, as open weights. DeepSeek-R1 shipped under MIT in January 2025 and the V4 generation kept MIT in 2026. DeepSeek-V2 and the first V3 release used a more restrictive model license, and V3 moved to MIT in March 2025. The trend has been toward greater openness.


What's the largest open-source LLM?


Kimi K3 (2.8 trillion parameters, July 2026) is the largest open-weight model to date, followed by Alibaba's Qwen3.8 flagship (2.4 trillion) and DeepSeek V4 Pro (about 1.6 trillion). All three are mixture-of-experts, so only a fraction of the parameters run per token.


Is Meta still releasing open models?


Yes. After Llama 4 in April 2025 and the closed Muse Spark in April 2026, Meta released Muse Spark Open on October 15, 2026: 816 billion total and about 42 billion active parameters under the Muse Model License.


What is the OSI Open Source AI Definition?


It is the Open Source Initiative's 2024 standard (version 1.0, October 28, 2024) for open source AI. A system must be usable, studyable, modifiable and shareable, which requires the weights, the full code and detailed training data information under OSI-approved terms.


What was the first open mixture-of-experts LLM?


Mixtral 8x7B (December 2023, Apache 2.0) was the first open mixture-of-experts model most developers used, with 46.7 billion total and about 12.9 billion active parameters.


Which open-source LLM licenses allow commercial use?


Apache 2.0 and MIT models (Mistral, most Qwen sizes, DeepSeek-R1 and V4, GLM-5, gpt-oss, Gemma 4) allow commercial use freely. Llama adds a 700 million monthly user clause, and 2026 flagships such as Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 and Muse Spark Open add terms for large API resellers.


Are open models as good as GPT-5 or Claude?


On many tasks, yes, and the gap is down to months. The top proprietary models still lead on the hardest reasoning and on reliability. Most teams use both and route per task.


Can I run these locally?


Small open-weight models run on a single GPU or laptop; the biggest (like Kimi K3) need data-center hardware even with open weights. Managed platforms like Taskade Genesis let you use them without any setup.


How much memory do I need to run an open-source LLM?


About 2 bytes per parameter at 16-bit, 1 byte at 8-bit and half a byte at 4-bit, plus context cache. A 7B model at 4-bit needs about 4 to 5 GB, and a 70B model about 40 GB.
